lines: The rain has lifted. Three lengths of pipe are missing from the supply ledger. Someone crossed out a name. Nobody agrees whose.
{player}, you used to ask why I never let you rub out a mistake. Today you get the longer answer.
There's a terminal in the ridge office. I have a battery, two good leads, and a courier who has repeated my instructions so often I no longer like them.
You have a screen. That's what you have. Last time, a screen said the gate was ready. My sister went downstream to check.
We are not connecting a gate. We are going to print a receipt. Something small enough for all of us to check.
And who decides what counts as checked?

choices.label: I'll keep a repair log you can inspect.
Let me show you the screen before I make a promise.
Stand beside me. You can stop the trial.

lines: Write down what you expect before you try it. Not just what happened to work.
A fair condition. Keep the crossed-out lines too.
I chose {language} because I want to {intent}.
Then start with a line you can explain. The terminal is beyond the stone path. Wick has my note.
A demonstration has an audience. A test has a way to be wrong. Bring me the second one.
He isn't asking you to fail. He's asking you to know what failure would look like.
I chose {language} because I want to {intent}.
The terminal is beyond the stone path. Read Wick's note, then try one instruction.
All right. I keep the battery lead where I can reach it. You tell me before you change anything.
Two people, one small trial. That will do.
I chose {language} because I want to {intent}.
The terminal is beyond the stone path. Wick has my note. He cannot explain it, but he is very persistent.
WICK · A PAPER NOTE FROM MARA
First: make the terminal display Ready. Second: learn how it reads a whole line. Third: print an item name and record it.
If you don't understand a symbol, ask what it does. Copying a line is how you begin. Explaining why it works is how you keep it.
{guidance} Press F2 whenever you want to practice. Nothing in the ruins takes that away.
You promised a repair log. Start with a plain claim: what should happen, and what would tell you it didn't?
A missing page bothers me more than an honest mistake.
I haven't forgotten. You wanted to show me something before making a promise.
When you come back, tell me what the machine still cannot do.
The lead is here. We stop if we smell hot insulation. No gate. No pump. Just a screen.
You asked me to stand beside you. I'm standing.
Ready. Good. Tell me what you've proved.

choices.label: Only that it prints the word I told it to print.
It works. We should try something bigger.
Let Rook pick the next test.

lines: A status message is a claim made by a program. A test is evidence about that claim. Keep the difference.
Now the receipt. Not just Rope: Copper wire, with its space still in it. We need the whole item name.
If I paint READY on the gate, have I repaired its hinge?
We have proved output, not safety. The next job is still small: read an item name and print a receipt.
Show me a case you expect to fail. Then show me how you corrected it.
An item name with a space. The ledger says Copper wire. A record of Copper is a different record.
That is a useful test. Read a whole line. Make a receipt somebody else can recognize.
And try a second name. I'd like to know the first one wasn't a lucky guess.
Item: Copper wire. Recorded. And the other names work too.
This does not settle who took the pipe. It gives us a record whose rules we can inspect.
There's something about the old sluice trial I should have told you before today.

choices.label: Tell me what happened to Ada.
Keep the record. We'll read it together when you're ready.

lines: I signed the trial sheet. The machine printed Ready after loading its settings. We treated that as proof the sensor was calibrated.
I kept the sheet. Keeping it didn't make me answer for it. I know that now.
Tomorrow we read the rest. Today you made one thing we can check. Let that be enough.
The sheet is in my locked drawer. I signed it. You should know that much now.
Today you made one thing we can check. Let that be enough.
The opening chapter ends here. The Java expedition continues in the workbench. The next story chapter will ask what happens when a working rule meets a bad reading.
